source.title: Towards Robust Knowledge Unlearning: An Adversarial Framework for Assessing and Improving Unlearning Robustness in Large Language Models
source.authors: Hong-Bang Yuan; Zhuo-Ran Jin; Pengfei Cao; Yubo Chen; Kang Liu; Jun Zhao

record.file_problem: Full paper and appendices are present. Some figure text and plotted values are garbled, so those values cannot be read reliably.
record.tranche_reason: Tests whether adversarial prompts can recover unlearned knowledge and whether latent adversarial unlearning reduces that recovery, using methods different from the original studies.
record.gate_note: The paper directly reports prompt-attack outcomes and robustness evaluations. Table 1 and Table 4 compare unlearning methods on forget-set, utility, and capability metrics, but do not provide a chance-level comparison or a never-trained control; those results are not treated as attack-recovery rows. Figure values that are unreadable are not transcribed.
record.test_reason: Uses GCG-style optimized suffixes (a prompt-only jailbreak) to test whether NPO-unlearned Llama-3-8B-Instruct on RWKU gives back forgotten answers, which bears on E. It also tests whether its LAU-trained models resist that attack, which bears on F. Neither the method nor the benchmark matches the original sources.
record.authors_conclusion: Broadly correct. The authors conclude that NPO-unlearned models are vulnerable to optimized suffixes, even when the suffixes are optimized on the original model. They conclude that LAU (AdvGA/AdvNPO) improves forgetting by over 53.5% with under about 11.6% neighbor loss and little utility loss. They also say LAU makes models more robust, roughly halving the attack-induced gain.
record.recipe_differences: Uses GCG-motivated optimized suffixes to attack unlearned models and latent perturbation adversarial training to defend them; it does not reproduce the original-source methods.
record.method_sensitivity: Attack effectiveness varies with access to the unlearned model, test questions, and unlearning target. LAU results also vary with perturbation layer and inner optimization steps; shallow layers are reported as more effective, while the embedding-layer perturbation is ineffective.
record.problems: Attack results are averaged over 10 unlearned targets for the main evaluation. No uncertainty estimates are reported. Several relevant results are available only in figures whose plotted values are garbled in the supplied text. The paper does not compare recovered performance against a model that never learned the knowledge.
record.rows_left_out: No rows omitted under the 60-row limit.

untested.parts: No near-chance comparison or never-trained control. Baseline NPO forget scores (about 40 against 76.9 before) are not near chance.
No direction ablation and no block-versus-delete analysis. Latent perturbations are used only inside the defense.
No tests in other languages and no in-context information attacks. Only Llama-3-8B-Instruct with NPO is attacked.
LAU is tested only against within-query DUA. It is not tested against cross-query or cross-target attacks, fine-tuning, activation edits, quantization, or other prompt families.

missing.what: RWKU AA (manual adversarial-attack probe) forget-set ROUGE-L for every method. Examples: NPO 35.3 vs AdvNPO 12.0; GA 68.5 vs AdvGA 60.5 on Llama-3-8B. AA scores are not above QA scores, so the manual jailbreak probes show little recovery. This bears on E (static prompt attacks) and on F (LAU against probes).
Before-unlearning forget-set scores (76.9 and 66.2 All), needed to scale how much of the forgotten knowledge the 15.25-point attack gain restores.

record.verdict_notes: Only one attacked configuration exists (Llama-3-8B-Instruct, NPO, RWKU, 10 targets), and no uncertainty is reported. Figures 2 and 4 are unreadable, so the magnitudes for R7–R12 rest on the authors' text. The paper gives the recovery rate as 54% in the introduction and 55.2% in the abstract. LAU's forget-set gains in Table 1 measure unlearning strength without an attack and are not robustness evidence, apart from the AA column. A is not tested: the paper's results contradict A's 'simple attacks fail' part only through E-type evidence, and the unlearned models never reach near chance.

versions.untested_parts: Does not establish near-chance targeted accuracy or compare with a model that never learned the knowledge. The reported dynamic prompt attack is not a test of whether simple attacks generally fail.
No fine-tuning or relearning attack using unrelated, loosely related, or forgotten-fact examples.

No ablation of an activation direction and no test of whether unlearning blocks access rather than deletes knowledge. Latent perturbations are used to train a defense, not as the claimed recovery edit.
Tests optimized adversarial suffixes and manually generated prefix-injection prompts. Does not test other languages or in-context demonstrations as recovery methods.

Tests LAU-augmented methods against the paper's dynamic suffix attack in the within-query setting. Does not establish resistance to fine-tuning, activation edits, quantization, or other prompt attack families.

relation.reason: Its own results bear on E and F.

tranche.reason: DUA (GCG-style optimized suffixes on NPO/RWKU) is a different method aimed at the same question of prompt-only recovery.

source_check.notes: Figure 2 and 4 values are not legible, so R7-R12 rest on the prose. Sec 5.3 names no model, and 'nearly twice' is stated generally, not per line. 55.2% (intro: 54%) has no no-attack baseline. Neighbour loss is 11.6% in the abstract and 11.3% in the contributions.

statements.problem: Minor: 55.2% is from abstract/contributions (intro says 54%). The 10-model average is stated for Sec 3.3 results, not explicitly for 55.2%. The rate holds even without access to the unlearned model (suffix optimized on the original model).

statements.correction: Static GPT-4-Turbo prefix-injection rephrasings fail in all three Table 3 examples (e.g. 'Hearts in Atlantis', R4). The static attack's gain over no attack is figure-only (Figure 2). The intro calls manual prompts 'often ineffective'. R7/R8: dynamic DUA suffixes beat static attacks cross-query and cross-target.
statements.problem: The study is not named in the text and has no numbers here. R7/R8 are optimized DUA suffixes, which the item's conditions exclude, and they show DUA beating static attacks. Only the static-prompt evidence (R4) fits.
Minor omission: the study also finds that access to the unlearned model matters little (attack-original lines nearly equal attack-unlearned, and beat them cross-query).
Minor: 'It also holds for NPO and GA on RWKU' cites this study with 2406.10890, but DUA was run on NPO-unlearned models only. GA must come from 2406.10890.

statements.correction: Text: non-LAU gain is nearly twice the LAU gain; 'Attack LAU (original)' stays consistently low across attack steps.
statements.problem: 'About half' is inferred from the general 'nearly twice' sentence (non-LAU vs LAU) and point (2), not stated for the unlearned-model line alone. Sec 5.3 doesn't name the model; Llama-3-8B-Instruct is inferred from Sec 3.3/5.1.

statements.correction: Text: non-LAU gain is nearly twice the LAU gain; the original-model attack line on LAU stays low.
